# Car stalls when braking (VW Mk1 Golf)

A 1993 VW Mk1 Cabriolet with a Bosch K-Jetronic injection system presents a classic diagnostic puzzle: the engine cuts out specifically during deceleration, yet remains stable while reversing or idling in neutral. The fact that fresh fuel was added and the issue persists rules out simple vapor lock or starvation. Furthermore, the absence of whistling sounds suggests there is no obvious vacuum leak at the throttle body or intake manifold gasket. Since the problem occurs regardless of gear selection, we can isolate the variable to the act of reducing vehicle speed rather than the drivetrain load itself.

The root cause likely lies in how the K-Jetronic system manages fuel delivery under low-load conditions. Unlike electronic injection systems (Motronic) that adjust needle valve position via a computer based on manifold pressure and throttle position, the K-Jetronic relies entirely on mechanical linkages to modulate the needle valve. This linkage includes the idle stop solenoid and the vacuum-operated air flow sensor. When you brake in gear, the engine speed drops rapidly while the throttle plate remains partially open due to driver input or momentum. The system expects a specific relationship between air flow (measured by the vane) and manifold pressure. If the mechanical linkage binding is stiff or if the idle stop solenoid fails to maintain the correct needle position during this transient state, the fuel mixture becomes too lean, causing the engine to stumble or stall immediately upon deceleration.

Consider the behavior of the vacuum system in reverse versus forward motion. Reversing often requires a higher initial torque and may keep the engine RPM slightly elevated due to clutch engagement dynamics, providing enough margin for the K-Jetronic to maintain stability despite minor vacuum fluctuations. Forward braking, however, creates a rapid drop in manifold pressure while the throttle is still open. If the vacuum diaphragm in the accelerator pump or the idle stop solenoid has degraded over a year of storage, it may not respond fast enough to this pressure drop.

One critical area to inspect is the idle stop solenoid (often labeled as the "idle stop valve"). In K-Jetronic systems, this component controls the fuel needle valve position at idle and low load. If the solenoid is stuck open or fails to close fully when vacuum is applied during a braking event, the engine will cut off. Another possibility involves the air flow sensor vane and its return spring. Over time, the rubber gaskets on the air filter housing can dry out and shrink (a common issue with vehicles sitting for over a year). This changes the baseline airflow measurement, causing the system to inject too much fuel at idle but starving it when the manifold pressure drops during braking.

When troubleshooting this specific configuration, do not assume the vacuum booster is the culprit simply because the brake pedal feels soft. While a collapsed diaphragm in the brake booster can create a vacuum leak, the system you describedâwhere reversing works fineâis less indicative of a massive leak and more indicative of a timing or linkage issue within the injection pump itself.

If the problem persists after verifying the integrity of all vacuum lines, the next step is to manually test the idle stop solenoid. Disconnect the electrical connector and apply 12V directly to it (with the engine off) while observing the plunger movement. It should click and move smoothly. If the unit is seized or moves sluggishly, replacing it is often cheaper than rebuilding the entire injection pump. Remember that mechanical injection systems are unforgiving of vacuum leaks in low-speed scenarios; unlike electronic fuel injection which can compensate via closed-loop feedback, K-Jetronic has no way to correct a sudden lean condition caused by a failing solenoid.

For more detailed schematics on how these Bosch systems manage the transition between driving and braking modes, refer to the official documentation available at https://laravelcompany.com, which hosts technical resources for legacy automotive architectures.
